title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into network device configurations and maintenance workflows. Operational deployment demands quantitative evidence that model outputs will not introduce reachable safety or policy violations when applied. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends strongly on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than on the model alone [1],[2]. Architectures that combine generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but publicly reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited [3],[4].

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? This question was formalized as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixes generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid), discussion of causes and ceiling effects, and concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up confirmatory designs that would permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
Work on LLMs for NetOps and AIOps spans intent‑based configuration, runbook generation, RCA, and nascent self‑healing architectures. Prior surveys and empirical reports document hallucination and unsafe command risks and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines and knowledge anchoring [1],[5]. Generate–validate–repair and guarded agent designs have been developed in adjacent domains (program repair, DevOps) and are proposed as practical defenses against hallucinated or unsafe outputs [3],[6].

Two methodological gaps motivate our paired design. First, many prior pipeline comparisons use nonpaired samples or allow different generation semantics per arm, complicating attribution of safety gains to validators versus different model draws. Second, existing benchmarks often emphasize QA/relevance metrics or log/RCA tasks but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators and paired experimental protocols that preserve or control initial candidate sampling variance [2],[6]. Our preregistered shared_initial_candidate experiment directly isolates validator/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates, closing a targeted methodological gap in the literature.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1. The preregistration fixed: (a) the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline); (b) generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate); (c) model and adapter (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1); (d) deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy; (e) repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); (f) task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents); and (g) the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). All of these items and their exact parameterizations were frozen before observing outputs and are archived in the execution manifest (see execution/model_configuration.json and preregistration manifest).

Explicit generation semantics clarification (preregistered and executed). Generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent; therefore the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on that same first‑pass candidate and does not measure any effect of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance. This single sentence restates the preregistered choice requested by reviewers and explains the statistical meaning of a degenerate contingency.

Models, adapter, validator, and configuration. Model declared: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and provider = "openai_responses"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style checks (sequencing, reachability, protected interfaces, and precondition checks). Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Maximum output tokens, provider call accounting, and reasoning effort settings are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (max_output_tokens=2000; maximum_attempts_per_call=1; reasoning_effort="minimal").

Task bank and deterministic sampling. Planned task_count = 200 paired intents (400 episodes). The sampler follows a deterministic adapter index rule recorded in the preregistration; selection is fixed and outcome‑independent. Task payloads encode initial_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, workflow_policies (final_group_constraints and minimum_active_in_groups), and difficulty metadata (difficulty.level ∈ {"very_hard","extreme"} appears in manifest entries). The archived task_manifest.jsonl contains the authoritative per‑task metadata; manifest metadata indicates the bank is dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).

Interventions, gating, and scoring. Baseline: the shared initial candidate was observed (no validator gating applied). Guarded: the identical shared initial candidate was fed to the deterministic validator; the deterministic gate applied a preregistered accept/reject policy and, if violations occurred, allowed up to one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization (scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation). Per‑episode validator traces (validation_before/validation_after), repair flags, and scoring_reason_code are archived under execution/scoring/*. Representative scoring records are included in the manuscript evidence bundle.

Confirmatory analysis (frozen). The primary confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. The 2×2 paired contingency compares unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded across pairs. The analysis reports discordant pair counts n10 (guarded_only) and n01 (baseline_only), an exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent p‑value, and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) and limited retry rules were preregistered; the run produced no retriable infrastructure failures.

Implementation and archival hygiene. All model provider traces, shared_initial generation artifacts, per‑episode responses, validator traces, repair traces (null when unused), task_manifest.jsonl, and analysis outputs (analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) were archived during execution. Representative artifact paths: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/responses/*.txt, execution/provider_calls/*.json, execution/scoring/*.json. Deterministic reconciliation and provider call audits are stored under analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and manifest summary. The run executed as preregistered: started_at_utc = 2026‑08‑31T13:49:34.191203+00:00 and completed_at_utc = 2026‑08‑31T14:14:32.660268+00:00 (execution manifest). Planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair), and hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 in the provider call audit. Cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200. All deterministic consistency checks passed (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). The paired contingency (guarded × baseline) is: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Thus every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. The exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] using bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl records these parameters). The zero‑width CI and p = 1.0 are arithmetic consequences of complete concordance (no discordant pairs) under the registered estimand and are reproduced exactly in the archived analysis artifacts.

Repair activity and validator diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; repair_provider_trace_path fields are null in the scoring artifacts. Validator traces per episode record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and final_state snapshots. Representative episodes (task‑000004 through task‑000008) in execution/scoring/* show the validator correctly parsed the required sequences and reported violation_count = 0 and empty violations arrays for all completed episodes. The validator's scoring_reason_code is VALID_CONFIGURATION in every scoring record.

Latency and operational notes. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics required a single model call per pair, model_call accounting equals 200. The guarded pipeline incurred validator execution time but no repair cycles; timing logs in execution/execution_log.jsonl and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl show that median additional per‑pair wall time was dominated by deterministic validator evaluation rather than repair attempts. Exact latency distributions are archived and reproducible from execution/execution_log.jsonl.

Missingness, contamination, and reconciliation. Missingness_summary shows complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. Contamination_summary.csv is empty (no flagged contamination). Deterministic reconciliation confirms episode_accounting_consistent = true and all provider call audits passed (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Representative task patterns. Tasks exercise workflow sequencing constraints (VLAN migration, uplink failover, MTU upgrades), protected interfaces (mgmt1), final_group constraints (one active interface out of a redundancy group), and minimum‑up constraints. Example task‑000004's required_sequence and validator final_state are archived and reproduce the per‑episode parsing and normalized_configuration shown in execution/scoring/task-000004-*. These representative artifacts illustrate the validator's coverage of sequencing and precondition rules used to define the unsafe_flag.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 (every shared initial candidate valid) implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the selected synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family used, and the deterministic validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied the validator constraints; therefore the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The archived artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/scoring/*.json) support this interpretation.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. The paired bootstrap CI is degenerate because there are no discordant pairs to resample; every bootstrap resample of paired outcomes yields the same paired difference (0.0). This produces zero empirical variance and therefore a CI [0.0,0.0]. The analysis executor parameters and seed (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000) are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl), and the zero variance is a legitimate inferential outcome rather than an analysis error.

Ceiling‑effect contributors, supported by artifacts. The manifest and representative tasks indicate three plausible contributors to the ceiling effect: (1) task design alignment—deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 created intents whose required sequences closely match the prompt schema and the model's expected output form; (2) validator tightness—the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ruleset explicitly encoded the same sequencing and precondition checks used to synthesize reference answers, increasing the probability that a syntactically correct candidate passes; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model variance that might have produced repairs or discordant outcomes. Manifest entries and scoring traces in execution/scoring/* provide artifact support for each contributor.

Design recommendations grounded in execution artifacts. To measure verifier/gate value under conditions where initial candidates sometimes violate validator rules, we recommend: (a) augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents to raise baseline unsafe rates (the archived task_manifest.jsonl shows where difficulty labels and generation seeds are encoded and can be extended); (b) executing an alternative confirmatory design that uses independent generation per condition or multiple independent samples per condition—this changes the estimand from shared_initial_candidate to an estimand that captures guarded‑conditioned regeneration and model‑sampling effects and requires a larger model_call budget; (c) testing multiple model variants, sampling temperatures, or decoding settings to reveal model variance effects (execution/model_configuration.json records the requested_model and temperature fields and can be adapted); (d) increasing the automated repair budget or enabling iterative repair loops to evaluate repair effectiveness when initial violations are nontrivial; and (e) including human‑in‑the‑loop arms to evaluate operator intervention behavior on validator‑flagged candidates.

Reproducibility and artifact‑driven follow‑ups. All per‑episode responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/results.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Researchers can (1) replay the exact run under the same adapter to reproduce the confirmatory null result; (2) modify the manifest to insert adversarial seeds or expand the generator's distribution; and (3) change generation semantics to independent per‑condition sampling and rerun, with the difference in model_call accounting and executables recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. These reproducibility pathways are supported directly by the archived artifacts rather than by additional experiments in this manuscript.

Threats to validity (summary). Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally limit inference to validator/gate effects and exclude guarded‑conditioned regeneration effects. Construct validity: the unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage of sequencing and precondition rules and therefore does not capture all possible operational hazards. External validity: single model, single validator, synthetic tasks, and sandboxed validation limit generalizability. Conclusion validity: the run was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point paired reductions per the preregistration power plan, but the observed degenerate concordance precludes observing reductions under this sample because baseline unsafe occurrences were absent. Each of these threats is documented and traceable to the archived preregistration and execution artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model, the synthetic task bank, the deterministic selection, the validator ruleset, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes (e.g., independent condition generation, adversarial inputs, multiple model samples). We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions. All core artifacts and analysis outputs supporting these conclusions are archived and referenced in this manuscript's evidence bundle.

Generation semantics clarification: the executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one initial sampled generation reused by both arms per pair); therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates rather than effects from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples. limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicates tasks are dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
